idiom_name: String.intern() and JDK boxed-value caches; ConcurrentHashMap or WeakHashMap pool for custom flyweights
implementation_notes: The JVM already runs the factory for the two hottest cases: String.intern() returns the canonical representation of an equal character sequence, and Integer.valueOf caches -128..127 as the language specification requires, so autoboxing reuses instances (Boolean.valueOf and Character.valueOf behave the same way); enum constants are canonical singletons by construction. For your own intrinsic state, hold it in an immutable class with final fields and pool it with ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent, or with a WeakHashMap or a weak-value interner when entries should be collectable. The extrinsic state lives in the caller's object. Interning shares whole values, however - it does not split your object's state into intrinsic and extrinsic parts, which remains the design work.
pitfalls: String.intern() is a native, process-wide table whose entries live as long as the JVM: interning request-derived, user-supplied or secret strings retains them forever and is a denial-of-service and disclosure vector. Use a bounded or weak pool instead.
Interning makes identity (==) meaningful for equal values, which breaks code that assumed equal-but-distinct objects and quietly endangers any design that mutates the shared instance.
Integer.valueOf caches only the mandated -128..127 range (configurable upward); relying on reference identity outside that range - or on new Integer(...) ever being canonical - is a bug.

A static ConcurrentHashMap pool is an eternal strong reference and leaks with unbounded keys; computeIfAbsent also holds the bin while the mapping function runs, so never build the value through a slow call path.
